client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on me all day, and I can't seem to shake it no matter what I do. But honestly, what's weighing on me even more is watching my mom fall apart, and I have no idea how to be there for her when I'm barely holding it together myself.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is so heavy — your own grief, and then the added weight of feeling responsible for holding your mom up too, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling stretched so thin. I want to gently notice something you said: that you need to be there for her *when you're barely holding it together* — which suggests a part of you believes you have to be fully okay before you're allowed to support someone else. What do you think it would actually look like to grieve *alongside* your mom, rather than having to be strong *for* her?

client: I hear what you're saying, but I honestly don't know if I can let myself fall apart in front of her — she's my mom, and seeing me struggle would just add to her pain, I think. Like, there's this unspoken rule in our family that someone has to be the steady one, and I've always been that person. The idea of grieving "alongside" her sounds nice in theory, but in practice I can't picture what that even looks like without it turning into a mess where we're both drowning.
therapist: That role of being "the steady one" sounds like it's been part of your identity for a long time, and right now it might feel like the most loving thing you can do — but I'm also hearing how isolating and exhausting it is to carry that, especially while you're grieving yourself. It's worth gently questioning that unspoken rule: is it actually true that showing your own sadness to your mom would add to her pain, or is it possible it might even help her feel less alone in hers? What do you think that belief about needing to stay steady is costing you right now?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows there's probably some truth to it. But I genuinely worry that if I break down in front of my mom, she'll feel like she has to take care of me instead of the other way around, and that feels selfish when she's the one who just lost her husband. The cost of staying steady... I guess it's that I feel completely alone in my grief, like I'm mourning my dad in secret while everyone else gets to fall apart openly.
therapist: That image of mourning in secret is really poignant, and it sounds quietly heartbreaking — like you're standing just outside a room where everyone else gets to grieve together, but you've locked yourself out to protect them. I want to reflect something back to you: you called it *selfish* to need support while your mom grieves, but you'd never call it selfish if she needed support from *you* — so there seems to be a different set of rules for what you're allowed to need. What do you think taught you that your grief matters less than everyone else's?

client: That image you used — standing outside the room — that actually hit me harder than I expected, because yeah, that's exactly what it feels like. But when you ask what taught me my grief matters less... I don't know, I think it's just always been that way, like I'm the one who holds things together so everyone else can fall apart. It feels less like something I was taught and more like just... who I am, and I'm not sure I even know how to be any different.
therapist: There's something both tender and a little sad in what you just said — that this role doesn't feel like a rule you follow, but like your actual identity, which makes it feel almost impossible to put down without losing a piece of yourself. But I want to sit with that word "always" for a moment, because most of the time when something feels like *who we are*, it started as something we *did* to survive or to keep love safe — and that's very different from it being your only way of existing. If the "steady one" is a role you stepped into rather than your whole self, what do you think the person underneath that role might actually need right now?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it — that there's some other version of me underneath all this that has needs too. But honestly, when I try to imagine that person, I just feel kind of... blank, or maybe scared, like if I'm not the one holding everything together, I don't really know who I am. And I think what that person needs is probably just to not feel so alone for once, but admitting that feels almost embarrassing, like I should be past needing that by now.
therapist: What you just said — that underneath everything, you just don't want to feel so alone — that's not embarrassing at all; that's one of the most deeply human needs there is, and the fact that you've been quietly carrying your grief while telling yourself you shouldn't need that is actually really painful. I also want to gently push back on "I should be past needing that by now," because that phrase carries a kind of harsh judgment toward yourself — as if needing connection has an expiration date, or as if you've somehow failed by still being human. Where do you think that "should" comes from — who taught you that needing others is something to grow out of?

client: I think that "should" probably came from my dad, honestly. He was always really big on self-sufficiency, like needing people was a sign of weakness, and I guess I just absorbed that without ever questioning it. Hearing you say it out loud like that... it's uncomfortable, because part of me still believes he was right, even though another part of me knows how lonely that way of thinking has made me.
therapist: It takes real courage to name that, especially so soon after losing him — because now you're holding both your love for your dad *and* the recognition that something he taught you has quietly kept you isolated, and that's a genuinely complicated and tender place to be. What's so important is that you can already see the contradiction yourself: that his belief in self-sufficiency, which he may have passed on with love, has cost you the very connection that makes grief bearable. I'm wondering — if your dad could see the loneliness that rule has created in you, do you think he would still want you to hold onto it?

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because... no, I don't think he would. He wasn't a cruel man, he just thought he was teaching me strength. But it's hard to separate the lesson from him, you know? Like letting go of that rule feels almost like losing another piece of him.
therapist: What you just said is so important — that releasing this belief feels like another small loss of him, which makes it so much harder to question, because it's not just a rule anymore, it's a thread that still connects you to your dad. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if honoring him doesn't have to mean keeping the lesson exactly as he gave it, but instead taking the *intention* behind it — that he wanted you to be strong — and redefining strength in a way that actually includes letting yourself be loved and supported? What do you think *your* definition of strength might look like, one that your dad would recognize but that doesn't leave you so alone?

client: That's... a really hard question to sit with, because part of me wants to say yes, maybe strength can look different, but another part of me feels like I'd be putting words in his mouth, deciding what he "would have wanted" when he's not here to say. And honestly, that feels a little presumptuous, like I'm rewriting him to make myself feel better. I guess I'm scared that if I redefine it, I'm not actually honoring him anymore — I'm just letting myself off the hook.
therapist: That fear of "letting yourself off the hook" is really worth examining, because it reveals something important — that somewhere inside, you believe you *deserve* the loneliness and the burden, like suffering through it is a form of loyalty to him. But honoring someone and letting yourself heal aren't opposites; in fact, reexamining what he taught you *is* a form of deep engagement with who he was, not an erasure of him. I'm curious — if your dad had absorbed a painful belief from *his* father, would you want him to carry it forever out of loyalty, or would you want him to be free?

client: That question kind of stopped me cold, honestly. Like, of course I'd want my dad to be free from whatever his father passed down to him — I wouldn't want him suffering just to prove he loved someone. But it's easier to want that for him than to let myself have it, and I don't fully understand why that is.
therapist: You just gave yourself the answer — you wouldn't make your dad suffer to prove his love, and yet that's exactly the standard you're holding yourself to, which tells us something really significant: you can access profound compassion for the people you love, but there's a barrier that stops that same compassion from turning inward toward yourself. That gap — between what you'd freely give others and what you'll allow yourself — is often one of the most important things we can explore in this kind of work. What do you think that barrier is made of — what's the voice that says others deserve that freedom, but you don't quite?

client: I think the barrier is... this voice that says I should know better. Like, my dad didn't choose to get sick, so of course he deserves compassion — but I chose to pull away from people, I chose to let those friendships fade, so I don't get the same pass. It feels like there's a difference between suffering that happens to you and suffering you kind of created yourself.
therapist: That distinction you're making — between "innocent suffering" and suffering you feel responsible for — is such a common and painful way we deny ourselves compassion, but I want to gently challenge it: the choices you made to pull away from people didn't come from nowhere, they came from a belief system you absorbed as a child that told you needing others was weakness, which means even those "choices" were shaped by something that happened *to* you. Holding yourself solely responsible for the loneliness, without accounting for the lessons that drove those decisions, is a little like blaming someone for limping without acknowledging they were taught to walk that way. What do you think it would take for you to see those choices with the same understanding you'd extend to someone else who'd been taught the same things your dad taught you?
